messages.text: I keep thinking I wasn’t supposed to make it past 2020. Like I’m here by accident and I don’t know why.

It sounds like you’re feeling disconnected from your own survival, and maybe unsure about your purpose right now. Those thoughts can be scary and heavy, especially if they make you question why you’re still here. You are not here by accident—your life has meaning even if it’s hard to see in this moment. Can you share what 2020 meant for you and why that year feels like a turning point?
It was the year everything cracked. I don’t know if I’m meant to still be here. Faith says otherwise, but some days it feels like I’m just… borrowing time.

It’s understandable to feel that way after a year that brought so much loss and upheaval—it can leave deep cracks in how we see ourselves and the future. Faith telling you there’s meaning might offer comfort sometimes, but it can also clash with the weight of those “borrowing time” feelings. You’re allowed to wrestle with both hope and doubt. Would it feel safe to talk about what “borrowing time” looks like in your day-to-day life?
I just keep coming back to that thought — like it’s a fact, not a feeling. I made it through, but I don’t know why I did when so much in me wanted to let go.

It sounds like that thought has become fixed in your mind, and carrying it might make survival feel confusing or even undeserved. Making it through despite wanting to let go can be both painful and powerful—it speaks to a resilience you may not fully recognize yet. I want to check: are you feeling any urge to harm yourself right now, or is this more about remembering those past feelings? Your safety matters, and we can talk about what’s keeping you here in this moment.
I don’t want to die, but I’m not sure I truly want to live either. It’s like I’m stuck in between.

Feeling caught between not wanting to die and not feeling fully invested in living can be exhausting. That “in‑between” space often comes with numbness and uncertainty, but it can also be a starting point for exploring what might add meaning. You’ve already shown you can endure hard moments, so finding small anchors could help shift the balance. Would you like to talk about what gives you even a momentary sense of connection or relief?
I’ve been sleeping a lot again. Like, 14 hours and still tired. It’s easier than facing the day.

Sleeping that much can be a way to avoid the heaviness you’re feeling, but it might also signal your body and mind are struggling. Excessive sleep can deepen fatigue and create a loop that makes facing the day even harder. You don’t have to tackle everything at once—small, gentle steps can help break that cycle. Would you be open to exploring one manageable thing you could do after waking that feels safe and not overwhelming?
I don’t have the energy to try anything new. Even getting out of bed feels like too much.

It sounds like your energy is so low that even the smallest actions feel impossible, and that can be a sign you’re carrying more than your body and mind can handle alone. You don’t have to push yourself into “new” steps right now—sometimes the focus can just be on gentle survival. Have you shared this level of exhaustion with a healthcare provider or therapist? They could help identify both emotional and physical causes and work with you on relief.
I’ve tried therapy. It didn’t help. I’m not looking for another referral — I just needed you to know how heavy this feels right now.

I hear you, and it’s important that you’re being honest about how heavy things feel for you right now. Sometimes being witnessed without pressure to change can be the first step toward easing that weight. You’ve made it through moments like this before, even if it feels unbearable in the present. Would it feel okay for us to focus on ways to help you feel a little more grounded in this moment?
Is it normal to feel this hopeless and still be okay? I don’t want to be a burden.

It’s more common than you might think to feel hopeless yet not be in immediate danger, but that doesn’t make the pain any less real. Feeling like a burden can be a powerful barrier to reaching out, yet sharing your feelings is not something others see as burdensome—it’s part of human connection. You deserve care and support even in this in‑between space. Would you like to explore how hopelessness shows up for you and what might soften it bit by bit?
It just helps to say it out loud and not be told to fix it. I don’t have answers — I just needed someone to know it feels like I’m surviving on borrowed time.

I’m glad you’re telling me, and I’m hearing you without trying to push solutions. Naming that sense of “borrowed time” out loud can make it feel less isolating. You’re allowed to sit with the uncertainty and still be seen. Would you like me to simply stay with you in that feeling for a bit?
Yes. It helps that you’re not trying to fix it. Just… being here with it.

I’m here with you, holding that space so you don’t have to carry it alone. You don’t need to rush toward answers or force change right now. Your presence matters, even in this quiet and heavy place. We can stay here as long as you need.
Thank you. I don’t have the energy to fix anything right now. Just… thank you for not pushing.

You’re welcome, and it’s okay not to have the energy to fix anything right now. Sometimes simply being heard is enough for this moment. You don’t need to meet any expectations here. I’m here with you, just as you are.
